P2289
Severe worsening of the stiff person
syndrome due to acute gastroenteritis
M. G. Kramberger 1, A. Avber šek 2, T. Hojs Fabjan 3
1Neurology Hospital, University Medical Centre Ljubljana,
Ljubljana, 2Neurology Department, University Medical
Centre Maribor, 3Neurology Department, University Medical
Centre Maribor, Maribor, Slovenia
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare disorder characterized
by progressive rigidity of the axial muscles with
superimposed painful spasms precipitated by tactile stimuli,
passive stretch, and volitional movement of affected or
unaffected muscles, startling noises, and emotional stimuli.
A 54-year-old female with autoimmune thyroid disease,
presented with a 2 year history of stiffness of the lower spine
and gait problems that acutely worsened during acute viral
gastroenteritis. After one day of nausea, diarrhoea and
vomiting she developed severe painful spasms in lower limbs
and generalised, predominantly axial and proximal stiffness
with hyper-reflexia in the limbs and strong contraction of the
muscles of the abdomen, transient urinary retention,
tachycardia and hypertension. The epidemiological history
was positive. Urgent diagnostic workup excluded acute
abdomen and she reported some relief 30 minutes after
parenteral administration of diazepam. In the last year she
had three previous diagnostic evaluations due to episodic
painful spasms of truncal muscles, progressive gait
impairment, occasional falls and development of hyper-
lordosis, which confirmed no obvious cause. The symptoms
progressively partly improved with benzodiazepines until
they had partially remitted at three months. Additional
electromyography of trunk muscles demonstrated
simultaneous agonist and antagonist motor unit firing at rest,
and high serum titres of antibodies against glutamic acid
decarboxylase were confirmed. There was moderate
therapeutic response to high dose benzodiazepines, baclofen
and immunotherapy. To our knowledge this is the first
description of a patient with confirmed SPS who experienced
paroxysmal severe autonomic dysfunction and superimposed
“attacks” of intense muscle spasms following acute
gastroenteritis.
